title: Regulators & Power Supplies
description: Design unregulated supplies, linear and three-terminal regulators with heat sinks and protection, and buck, boost and inverting switching converters.

study.title: Explore: the unregulated supply
study.body: Transformer, bridge rectifier and reservoir capacitor give a DC voltage that peaks at $\sqrt2V_{rms}$ minus **two** diode drops. Between peaks the capacitor alone feeds the load, so it sags by $\Delta V \approx I/(f_rC)$, with $f_r$ = 100 Hz for full-wave rectification of 50 Hz mains. The diodes recharge $C$ in short, high current pulses, so pick a transformer VA rating of about 1.5–2× the DC power. Drag $C$ (load 1 A).

study.title: Linear regulator and dropout
study.body: A linear regulator compares a fraction of $V_{out}$ with a stable reference; the error amplifier drives a series **pass transistor** that drops the excess voltage. The loop holds $V_{out} = V_{ref}(1 + R_2/R_1)$. It only works while $V_{in}$ exceeds $V_{out}$ by the **dropout voltage**: about 2–2.5 V for an npn-Darlington pass device (78xx, LM317), 0.1–0.5 V for a **low-dropout (LDO)** regulator with a pnp or PMOS pass device. Check the dropout at the bottom of the ripple valley at low mains.

study.title: Three-terminal regulators
study.body: The 78xx (positive) and 79xx (negative) give fixed outputs (7805: +5 V, 1 A) with built-in current limit and thermal shutdown. The adjustable LM317 keeps 1.25 V between out and adj; $R_1$ (typically 240 Ω) sets a current through $R_2$. The small adj-pin current ($I_{adj} \approx$ 50 µA) adds $I_{adj}R_2$ to the output. Put 0.1–1 µF capacitors close to the input and output pins.

study.title: Dissipation and heat sinking
study.body: All the excess voltage turns into heat in the pass transistor, $P = (V_{in} - V_{out})I$, so the efficiency is at most $V_{out}/V_{in}$. Heat flows from junction to case to heat sink to air through thermal resistances (°C/W) that add like resistors in series. Keep $T_J$ below the maximum (typ. 125–150 °C) at the **highest** input voltage, load current and ambient temperature.

study.title: Protection and references
study.body:
- **Current limiting**: a sense resistor $R_{sc}$ turns on a transistor at $I_{lim} \approx 0.6\,\text{V}/R_{sc}$.
- **Foldback**: the limit falls as $V_{out}$ collapses, so a short dissipates far less.
- **Crowbar**: an SCR shorts the output when it exceeds a threshold, blowing the fuse.
- **References**: a bandgap reference gives ≈1.23 V with low drift; zeners around 5–6 V have nearly zero temperature coefficient.

study.title: Switching converters
study.body: A switcher chops the input with a transistor at duty cycle $D$ and filters it with an inductor and capacitor. An ideal switch and inductor waste no power, so efficiencies of 80–95 % are normal. The **buck** steps down, the **boost** steps up, and the **inverting buck-boost** gives $V_{out} = -V_{in}\frac{D}{1-D}$, a negative output of either size (all for continuous inductor current).

study.title: Switcher practicalities
study.body: In a buck the inductor current ripples by $\Delta I_L$ each cycle; a common choice is 20–40 % of $I_{out}$. By power balance the input current is only $I_{in} = V_{out}I_{out}/(\eta V_{in})$. Fast switching edges and pulsed currents make switchers **noisy** (conducted and radiated EMI at $f_{sw}$ and its harmonics), so sensitive analog circuits often get an LDO after the switcher. **Charge pumps** use switched capacitors instead of an inductor to invert or double a voltage at low currents.

steps.title: The unregulated supply
steps.body: A transformer, a bridge rectifier and a big reservoir capacitor turn mains into rough DC. The capacitor charges to $V_{pk} = \sqrt2V_{rms} - 2V_D$ (in a bridge, two diodes conduct in series) and sags between peaks while it feeds the load. With full-wave rectification the ripple frequency is 2 × 50 Hz = 100 Hz.

steps.prompt: A transformer secondary of {{Vr}} V rms feeds a bridge rectifier (0.7 V per diode) and a reservoir capacitor. What is the peak DC voltage with a light load?
steps.explanation: $V_{pk} = \sqrt2 V_{rms} - 2V_D$ = 1.414 × {{Vr}} V − 2 × 0.7 V = {{sqrt(2)*Vr|V|4}} − 1.4 V = **{{sqrt(2)*Vr-1.4|V}}**. Two diodes are in the current path in a bridge.

steps.prompt: A bridge rectifier on 50 Hz mains feeds a {{C|F}} reservoir capacitor; the load draws {{I|A}}. Estimate the peak-to-peak ripple.
steps.explanation: Full wave: $f_r$ = 100 Hz. $\Delta V \approx \frac{I}{f_rC}$ = {{I|A}} / (100 Hz × {{C|F}}) = **{{I/(100*C)|V}}**. (A rule of thumb: about 1 V of ripple per amp per 10 000 µF.)

steps.title: The linear regulator
steps.body: The op amp compares the divided output $V_{out}R_1/(R_1+R_2)$ with $V_{ref}$ and drives the pass transistor's base until they are equal. The transistor acts as a variable resistor in series with the load, burning off the excess voltage.

steps.prompt: In the series regulator, $V_{ref}$ = {{Vref|V}}, $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} (to ground) and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}}. Find $V_{out}$.
steps.explanation: The loop forces $V_{out}\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2} = V_{ref}$, so $V_{out} = V_{ref}(1 + R_2/R_1)$ = {{Vref|V}} × (1 + {{R2/R1||3}}) = **{{Vref*(1+R2/R1)|V}}**.

steps.prompt: Tap the resistors whose ratio sets the output voltage of this regulator.
steps.explanation: $R_1$ and $R_2$ divide $V_{out}$ down to $V_{ref}$, so $V_{out} = V_{ref}(1 + R_2/R_1)$. $R_{sc}$ is the current-sense resistor for current limiting (inside the loop, so it does not change $V_{out}$), and $R_L$ is the load.

steps.title: Where does the power go?
steps.body: The load current flows through the pass transistor, which has $V_{in} - V_{out}$ across it. That power is heat. Since input and output currents are (almost) equal, a linear regulator's efficiency is simply $V_{out}/V_{in}$.

steps.prompt: A linear regulator makes {{Vo|V}} at {{I|A}} from a {{Vin|V}} input.

ask.prompt: How much power does the regulator dissipate?
What is its efficiency in %?
ask.explanation: $\eta = \frac{V_{out}I}{V_{in}I} = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}$ = {{Vo}} / {{Vin}} = **{{100*Vo/Vin|%}}**. The load gets {{Vo*I|W}}, the regulator burns {{(Vin-Vo)*I|W}}.

steps.prompt: With a clever enough design, a linear regulator that drops 12 V to 5 V can reach 80 % efficiency.
steps.explanation: The pass device carries the full load current with 7 V across it, so the efficiency can never exceed $V_{out}/V_{in}$ = 5/12 = 42 %. Only a switching regulator, which stores energy in an inductor instead of burning it, can do better.

steps.prompt: A circuit needs a clean 3.3 V from a single Li-ion cell (4.2 V full, 3.6 V most of the time). Which regulator works?
options: A standard regulator with 2 V dropout
A 7805 with its output divided down
No regulator: just a series resistor
steps.explanation: Headroom is only 0.3–0.9 V. A standard npn-pass regulator needs about 2 V and would drop out; an LDO with a PMOS or pnp pass transistor regulates down to ~0.2 V headroom. A resistor does not regulate at all.

ask.prompt: Find $V_{out}$.
How large is the output-voltage error due to $I_{adj}$ alone?
ask.explanation: $I_{adj}$ flows through $R_2$ only: $I_{adj}R_2$ = 50 µA × {{R2|Ω}} = **{{50e-6*R2|V}}**, small next to the {{1.25*(1+R2/240)|V}} from the main term. That's why $R_1$ is kept small (it sets ≈5 mA through the divider).

steps.prompt: An LM317 must deliver {{Vo|V}} with $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}. Ignoring $I_{adj}$, what value must $R_2$ have?
A 7805 (5 V, needs 2 V headroom) is fed from a full-wave rectifier whose capacitor voltage peaks at {{Vpk|V}}. The load draws {{I|A}} (50 Hz mains).

ask.prompt: What is the largest ripple (peak-to-peak) you can allow?
ask.explanation: The ripple valley must stay at or above $V_{out} + V_{DO}$ = 5 + 2 = 7 V. So $\Delta V_{max}$ = {{Vpk}} − 7 = **{{Vpk-7|V}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the smallest reservoir capacitor?
ask.explanation: Allowed ripple: {{Vpk}} − (5 + 2) = {{Vpk-7|V}}. $C = \frac{I}{f_r\Delta V}$ = {{I|A}} / (100 Hz × {{Vpk-7|V}}) = **{{I/(100*(Vpk-7))|F}}**. Add margin for low mains and capacitor tolerance (−20 %).

steps.prompt: A 5 V regulator delivers {{I|A}} from {{Vin|V}}. $\theta_{JC}$ = {{tjc}} °C/W, $\theta_{CS}$ = 0.5 °C/W (thermal pad), heat sink $\theta_{SA}$ = {{tsa}} °C/W, ambient {{TA}} °C. Find the junction temperature in °C.

A regulator dissipates {{P|W}}. $T_{J,max}$ = 125 °C, $\theta_{JC}$ = {{tjc}} °C/W, $\theta_{CS}$ = 0.5 °C/W, ambient up to {{TA}} °C. What is the largest heat-sink thermal resistance $\theta_{SA}$ (in °C/W) you can use?
steps.explanation: Total allowed: $\theta_{JA} = \frac{T_{J,max} - T_A}{P}$ = (125 − {{TA}}) / {{P}} = {{(125-TA)/P||3}} °C/W. Subtract the rest of the chain: $\theta_{SA}$ = {{(125-TA)/P||3}} − {{tjc}} − 0.5 = **{{tsa||3}} °C/W**. Choose a heat sink with a lower value.

steps.prompt: A discrete regulator limits its current with a sense resistor and a transistor whose $V_{BE}$ turns on at 0.6 V.

ask.prompt: Which $R_{sc}$ gives a limit of {{Il|A}}?
ask.explanation: The limiter starts conducting when $I R_{sc}$ = 0.6 V: $R_{sc}$ = 0.6 V / {{Il|A}} = **{{0.6/Il|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: How much power does $R_{sc}$ dissipate at the {{Il|A}} limit?
ask.explanation: At the limit it has 0.6 V across it: $P$ = 0.6 V × {{Il|A}} = **{{0.6*Il|W}}**. This is also why a simple limiter costs ~0.6 V of extra headroom.

steps.prompt: A regulator with a {{Vin|V}} input has its output shorted to ground.

ask.prompt: With a simple current limit at {{Il|A}}, how much does the pass transistor dissipate?
ask.explanation: With $V_{out}$ = 0 the whole input voltage is across the pass transistor: $P = V_{in}I_{lim}$ = {{Vin}} V × {{Il|A}} = **{{Vin*Il|W}}**, much more than in normal use.

ask.prompt: With foldback limiting the short-circuit current drops to {{f*100}} % of {{Il|A}}. How much does it dissipate now?
ask.explanation: $I_{sc}$ = {{f}} × {{Il|A}} = {{f*Il|A}}, so $P$ = {{Vin}} V × {{f*Il|A}} = **{{Vin*Il*f|W}}** instead of {{Vin*Il|W}}. Foldback protects the transistor; the catch is that some loads (e.g. lamps, motors) may fail to start (latch-up).

steps.prompt: Match each circuit to what it does
pairs: Caps the output current at a set value
Lowers the current limit as V_out collapses
steps.explanation: Current limiting and foldback protect the regulator itself; a crowbar protects the **load** against an overvoltage (e.g. a shorted pass transistor) by firing an SCR and blowing the fuse; the bandgap reference combines a $V_{BE}$ (−2 mV/°C) with a PTAT voltage to get ≈1.23 V with almost zero drift.

steps.prompt: Which zener diode has the lowest temperature coefficient of its breakdown voltage?
steps.explanation: Below ≈5 V the zener effect dominates (negative TC), above ≈6 V avalanche breakdown dominates (positive TC, growing with voltage). Around 5–6 V the two cancel, so a 5.6 V zener drifts least. Precision references use bandgap circuits or temperature-compensated zeners.

steps.title: Buck, boost, inverting
steps.body: A switching converter only switches the transistor fully on or off, so it wastes little power. In steady state the inductor's average voltage is zero, which fixes the voltage ratio as a function of the duty cycle $D$ (fraction of the period the switch is on). The inverting buck-boost gives $V_{out} = -V_{in}\frac{D}{1-D}$.

steps.prompt: A buck converter makes {{Vo|V}} from {{Vin|V}}. What duty cycle does it run at (in %, ideal)?
A boost converter runs from {{Vin|V}} at a duty cycle of {{D*100}} %. What is its output voltage (ideal)?
steps.explanation: $V_{out} = \frac{V_{in}}{1-D}$ = {{Vin}} / (1 − {{D}}) = **{{Vin/(1-D)|V}}**. The output is always higher than the input.

steps.prompt: An inverting buck-boost converter runs from {{Vin|V}} at $D$ = {{D}}. What is $V_{out}$ (with sign)?
steps.explanation: $V_{out} = -V_{in}\frac{D}{1-D}$ = −{{Vin}} × {{D}}/{{1-D||2}} = **{{-Vin*D/(1-D)|V}}**. Below $D$ = 0.5 the magnitude is smaller than $V_{in}$, above it larger.

steps.prompt: A buck converter: {{Vin|V}} in, {{Vo|V}} out, $f_{sw}$ = {{f|Hz}}, $L$ = {{L|H}}. Find the peak-to-peak inductor ripple current.
steps.explanation: $D = V_{out}/V_{in}$ = {{D||3}}. During the on-time $DT$ the inductor sees $V_{in} - V_{out}$: $\Delta I = \frac{(V_{in} - V_{out})D}{f_{sw}L}$ = {{Vin-Vo||3}} V × {{D||3}} / ({{f|Hz}} × {{L|H}}) = **{{dI|A}}**.

steps.prompt: A buck converter delivers {{Vo|V}} at {{Io|A}} from {{Vin|V}} with an efficiency of {{eta*100}} %. What average current does it draw from the input?
steps.explanation: Power balance: $P_{in} = P_{out}/\eta$ = {{Vo*Io|W}} / {{eta}} = {{Vo*Io/eta|W}}. $I_{in} = P_{in}/V_{in}$ = {{Vo*Io/eta|W}} / {{Vin|V}} = **{{Vo*Io/(eta*Vin)|A}}**, less than the output current. A linear regulator would draw the full {{Io|A}}.

steps.prompt: You need 5 V at {{Io|A}} from {{Vin|V}}.

ask.prompt: How much heat does a linear regulator produce?
How much heat does a buck converter with {{eta*100}} % efficiency produce?
ask.explanation: $P_{loss} = P_{out}(1/\eta - 1)$ = {{5*Io|W}} × (1/{{eta}} − 1) = **{{5*Io*(1/eta-1)|W}}**, versus {{(Vin-5)*Io|W}} for a linear regulator.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the switch-node voltage of a buck converter ({{Vin|V}} input) and its average, which the LC filter passes to the output. Set the duty cycle for $V_{out}$ = {{Vo|V}}.
steps.explanation: The LC filter passes the average of the switch-node square wave: $V_{out} = DV_{in}$, so $D$ = {{Vo}} / {{Vin}} = **{{Vo/Vin||2}}**. In a real converter the control loop adjusts $D$ continuously to hold $V_{out}$ against input and load changes.

steps.prompt: What is the main reason switching regulators are 'noisy' compared to linear regulators?
options: Fast voltage and current edges at the switching frequency and its harmonics
The thermal noise of the inductor's winding resistance
The shot noise of the reference diode
The 100 Hz ripple of the rectifier
steps.explanation: The switch slams the node between 0 and $V_{in}$ in nanoseconds, and pulsed input/output currents flow through loops and capacitor ESR. This produces output ripple at $f_{sw}$, spikes at every edge, and conducted and radiated EMI up to high harmonics. Good layout, filtering and an LDO post-regulator tame it.

steps.prompt: A charge-pump inverter runs from {{Vin|V}}. It behaves like an ideal $-V_{in}$ source with an output resistance of {{Ro|Ω}}. What is $V_{out}$ (with sign) at a load current of {{I|A}}?
steps.explanation: $V_{out} = -(V_{in} - I R_{out})$ = −({{Vin}} − {{I|A}} × {{Ro|Ω}}) = −({{Vin}} − {{I*Ro}}) = **{{-(Vin-I*Ro)|V}}**. Charge pumps are simple and inductor-free but only suit small currents.

steps.prompt: Design a supply: an LM317 (needs 2.5 V headroom) delivers {{Vo|V}} at {{I|A}}. You allow {{dV|V}} ripple on the bridge-rectified (0.7 V diodes) reservoir capacitor, and the mains can be 10 % low.

ask.prompt: What reservoir capacitance do you need (50 Hz mains)?
What is the minimum transformer secondary voltage (rms, at nominal mains)?
ask.explanation: The valley must stay above {{Vo}} + 2.5 = {{Vo+2.5|V}}, so the peak must be {{Vpk|V}}, plus 1.4 V for the bridge: {{Vpk+1.4|V}} at low mains. At nominal mains: $V_{rms} = \frac{ {{Vpk+1.4}} }{0.9\sqrt2}$ = **{{Vr|V}}**. Then choose the next standard value up.

steps.prompt: A 5 V linear regulator at {{I|A}} is fed from a {{Vr}} V rms secondary with a bridge (0.7 V diodes) and {{dV|V}} ripple. Mains can be 10 % high.

ask.prompt: Estimate the average input voltage at high mains.
ask.explanation: Peak: 1.1 × √2 × {{Vr}} − 1.4 = {{1.1*sqrt(2)*Vr-1.4|V}}. The average sits about half the ripple below: {{1.1*sqrt(2)*Vr-1.4|V}} − {{dV/2|V}} = **{{Vav|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Estimate the regulator's worst-case dissipation.
ask.explanation: Average input at high mains ≈ 1.1 × √2 × {{Vr}} − 1.4 − {{dV/2}} = {{Vav|V}}. $P = (V_{in} - V_{out})I$ = ({{Vav||3}} − 5) × {{I}} = **{{P|W}}**. Size the heat sink for this, not for nominal mains.

steps.prompt: A 12 V, {{Q}} Ah battery powers a 3.3 V load drawing {{I|A}}.

ask.prompt: How many hours does it last with a linear regulator?
ask.explanation: A linear regulator draws the load current from the battery: $t = Q/I$ = {{Q}} Ah / {{I|A}} = **{{Q/I}} h**.

ask.prompt: How many hours does it last with a 90 %-efficient buck converter?

steps.prompt: A lossless boost converter (continuous inductor current) makes {{Vo|V}} at {{Io|A}} from {{Vin|V}}; $f_{sw}$ = {{f|Hz}}, $L$ = {{L|H}}.

ask.prompt: What is the duty cycle (in %)?
What is the average inductor (= input) current?
ask.explanation: Lossless: $V_{in}I_{in} = V_{out}I_{out}$ → $I_{in}$ = {{Vo}} × {{Io}} / {{Vin}} = **{{Iin|A}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the peak inductor current (average plus half the ripple)?
ask.explanation: $D$ = 1 − {{Vin}}/{{Vo}} = {{D||3}}. Average $I_L$ = {{Vo}} × {{Io}} / {{Vin}} = {{Iin|A}}. Ripple: $\Delta I = \frac{V_{in}D}{f_{sw}L}$ = {{Vin}} × {{D||3}} / ({{f|Hz}} × {{L|H}}) = {{dI|A}}. Peak = {{Iin|A}} + {{dI/2|A}} = **{{Iin+dI/2|A}}**. The switch and inductor must handle this without saturating.

steps.prompt: Choose the inductor of a {{Vin|V}} to {{Vo|V}} buck converter ({{Io|A}}, $f_{sw}$ = {{f|Hz}}) so the ripple current is 30 % of the output current.
steps.explanation: $\Delta I$ = 0.3 × {{Io|A}} = {{0.3*Io|A}}, $D$ = {{Vo}}/{{Vin}} = {{D||3}}. $L = \frac{(V_{in} - V_{out})D}{f_{sw}\Delta I}$ = {{Vin-Vo||3}} × {{D||3}} / ({{f|Hz}} × {{0.3*Io|A}}) = **{{L|H}}**. Higher $f_{sw}$ allows a smaller inductor (at the cost of switching losses).

steps.prompt: Put the steps of designing a linear bench supply in order
items: Fix output voltage, current and the regulator's dropout
Choose the allowed ripple and calculate the reservoir capacitor
Calculate the transformer voltage (low mains, diode drops)
Choose the heat sink from the thermal resistance chain
steps.explanation: Work backwards from the load: output and dropout set the minimum input; ripple sets $C$; the valley requirement at low mains sets the transformer; then high mains gives the worst-case dissipation, which sizes the heat sink.

steps.prompt: Match each requirement to the best supply solution
pairs: Low-noise ±15 V rails for an audio preamp, from mains
3.3 V at 10 mA from a 5 V USB supply
3.3 V at 3 A from a 48 V bus
−5 V at 10 mA from a +5 V rail
steps.explanation:
- A classic linear supply has no switching noise at all, and at preamp currents its dissipation is small.
- 5 V to 3.3 V at 10 mA: an LDO wastes only 17 mW; a switcher would be overkill.
- 48 V to 3.3 V at 3 A: a linear regulator would burn 134 W; only a buck converter makes sense.
- A small negative rail at low current: a charge pump needs no inductor.
